items.title: AMD-Powered Lux Supercomputer Opens to Scientific Users at Oak Ridge, Becoming First AI Factory for DOE’s Genesis Mission
items.content:
AMD-Powered Lux Supercomputer Opens to Scientific Users at Oak Ridge, Becoming First AI Factory for DOE’s Genesis Mission :: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)
Press Release
AMD-Powered Lux Supercomputer Opens to Scientific Users at Oak Ridge, Becoming First AI Factory for DOE’s Genesis Mission
November 16, 2026 2:00 pm EST
Download as PDF
AMD, ORNL and HPE bring AI and high-performance computing to researchers supporting the Genesis Mission.
News Highlights
Lux is ready for scientific users at Oak Ridge National Laboratory through a public-private partnership with AMD and the U.S. Department of Energy.
Lux brings together AMD EPYC CPUs, AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD Pensando networking and AMD ROCm software in a system built by HPE.
Genesis Mission projects allocated to run on Lux span fusion power plant design, materials development and manufacturing, and earth system prediction.
Lux is ranked 14
th
on today's TOP500 list of the world's most powerful supercomputers.
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov.  16, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today announced that the Lux SI + HPC supercomputer is open to scientific users at the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL).
Ranked 14
th
on today's TOP500 list of the world's most powerful supercomputers, Lux was developed through a public-private partnership between AMD and the DOE. The supercomputer provides the first dedicated U.S. AI Factory for the Genesis Mission, the DOE-led initiative to advance AI-driven science.
Lux brings together AMD EPYC™ processors, AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, AMD Pensando™ networking and AMD ROCm™ software in a system built by HPE. The system combines AI with high-performance modeling and simulation to expand U.S. capabilities in science, energy and national security.
“Lux shows what is possible when national laboratories, government and industry work together to advance scientific discovery. By bringing high-performance computing and AI closer to researchers, we are helping them explore new approaches to complex problems and make better use of simulation and experimental data. This partnership builds on a strong foundation at Oak Ridge and supports an open, sovereign AI stack with tools that can benefit researchers across the country,” said Thomas Zacharia, senior vice president, Global Public Sector and Strategic Partnerships, AMD.
“Lux represents the first major addition to DOE's computing infrastructure in support of the Genesis Mission, translating an ambitious national vision for SI-driven science into tangible capabilities for researchers,” said Georgia Tourassi, associate laboratory director for Computing and Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. “By expanding the computational resources available to the scientific community, Lux will help accelerate the integration of SI, modeling and simulation, and experimental data to advance discovery in areas critical to our nation’s energy, economic competitiveness and security.”
“Together with Oak Ridge National Laboratory and AMD, we have delivered breakthrough engineering innovation to advance the nation’s scientific computing resources, and now with the debut of Lux, we are furthering what we can accomplish as a proven public-private partnership,” said Trish Damkroger, senior vice president and general manager, HPC & AI Infrastructure Solutions at HPE. “We’re proud of our continued collaboration and investment in the Genesis Mission to stand up one of its first AI systems that will scale scientific research and make transformative breakthroughs to advance national initiatives.”
Expanding Computing Access for the Genesis Mission
The Genesis Mission
projects allocated to run on Lux include AI-assisted fusion power plant design, an AI-based foundation model factory for materials development and advanced manufacturing, and Earth system prediction to forecast water availability, streamflow and river temperature in the Tennessee Valley Authority region.
Lux marks the next chapter in the longstanding relationship among AMD, HPE, DOE and Oak Ridge to advance American science. Building on the computing foundation established at ORNL by the Frontier supercomputer, the first supercomputer to break the exascale barrier, Lux expands that foundation with dedicated capacity for AI-driven research. The upcoming Discovery supercomputer will extend this commitment with deeper integration of AI and high-performance computing. Together, these systems support the Genesis Mission by helping researchers connect simulation, AI and scientific data to accelerate discovery.
AMD is also working with ORNL to support DOE’s American Science Cloud, a national platform designed to extend advanced AI and high-performance computing capabilities across DOE laboratories, universities and mission partners in support of the Genesis Mission.
For researchers, Lux provides an opportunity to train and refine models using scientific data, to combine AI with established simulation methods, and to investigate problems that require computing beyond their home institutions. Its delivery extends the AMD and ORNL collaboration behind Frontier into dedicated capacity for AI-driven science.
Researchers and organizations interested in using Lux to advance Genesis Mission research are encouraged to contact ORNL’s Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (OLCF) to discuss their computing needs and applicable access pathways. Visit the
ORNL Lux resource page
to learn more about the system and connect with the OLCF team.

Press Release
AMD Completes Acquisition of World Labs
November 16, 2026 9:05 am EST
Download as PDF
News Highlights
Adds leading AI research team and deep model expertise to shape future AI infrastructure for the open ecosystem
Dr. Fei-Fei Li joins AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov.  16, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today announced the completion of its acquisition of World Labs, expanding its capabilities across the AI stack with a world-class model team. The acquisition brings together leading AI model researchers and AMD engineers to shape the next generation of AMD hardware, software and systems for the open AI ecosystem.
“Delivering the infrastructure that will power the next era of super intelligence requires us to optimize compute platforms and models together,” said Dr. Lisa Su, chair and CEO of AMD. “We are thrilled to welcome Fei-Fei Li and the exceptional World Labs team to AMD. Their pioneering model research will help shape our future hardware, software and systems. Together, we will enable researchers and developers across the ecosystem to push the boundaries of what AI can do.”
World Labs develops AI models that create and simulate interactive 3D environments, as well as technology for robotic learning and simulation. Dr. Fei-Fei Li joins AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist, reporting directly to Su.
The World Labs team will continue advancing foundational model research while collaborating with AMD engineers to apply insights from emerging model capabilities to the development of future AI infrastructure for customers and developers across the open AI ecosystem.

The offering consisted of 1,103,351,354 shares sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 shares sold by certain selling stockholders. The aggregate gross proceeds from the offering, before deducting underwriting discounts and commissions and other offering expenses, were approximately $93.5 billion, of which approximately $91.6 billion was received by Anthropic. Anthropic did not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares by the selling stockholders.
Anthropic’s Class A common stock began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19, 2026 under the symbol “ANT.”
In addition to the shares of Class A common stock sold in the initial public offering, Anthropic closed the concurrent sale of an aggregate of 313,253,007 shares of Class N common stock to Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., Broadcom Inc., Google LLC, Micron Technology, Inc., Microsoft Corporation, NVIDIA Corporation, and TSMC Partners, Ltd. at the public offering price of $83.00 per share, in a private placement for an aggregate purchase price of approximately $26.0 billion. The sale of these shares of Class N common stock was not registered under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “Securities Act”). Set up computer use for Team and Enterprise plans
Updated this week
Copy for LLM
Computer use lets Claude see a user's screen and work in the desktop apps they allow. Claude clicks and types like you would on Claude Desktop. This article explains how admins can turn computer use on for your organization, limit it to certain users, restrict it to specific apps, and manage it with device management (MDM).
Computer use is in beta on Team and Enterprise plans, and it's off by default. This is rolling out to organizations gradually.
Availability
Computer use works only in the new Claude experience, which is available where the
Chat and Cowork unified
capability is turned on. There, users can use it from:
Claude Desktop
, on macOS 14 or later and Windows.
Claude on the web and Claude Mobile
, if your organization's
Computer access
setting is on, with a computer that has Claude Desktop open.
It doesn't work in tasks started with the separate "Cowork" option, or in Claude Code. Owners can learn more in the article that applies to your plan:
Set up and manage the new unified Claude experience for your Team organization
Set up and manage the new unified Claude experience for your Enterprise organization
Organizations that can't turn on computer use include those with:
The HIPAA-ready configuration
Zero Data Retention (ZDR) for Claude Code
Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)
FERPA or K-12 settings
Note:
Computer use
and
Computer access
are different settings. Computer use lets Claude see the screen and work in apps. Computer access lets users reach their computer from scheduled tasks, Claude on the web, or Claude Mobile.
Before you turn on computer use
Review
Use Claude Cowork safely
and keep the following in mind:
Computer use has no sandbox between Claude and a user's applications. Content on the screen, such as web pages or emails, could cause Claude to take unintended actions.
Computer use isn't limited to the folders a user has connected. Through the apps a user approves, Claude can open, change, or delete files outside those folders.
If you
limit which folders users can connect
, that limit doesn't apply to computer use. Marking a folder "Read only" doesn't apply to computer use either.
If you're on an Enterprise plan and want to keep computer use from some users, read
Limit computer use to certain users
below before you turn it on.
Screenshots and your data
Claude takes screenshots to see and navigate the screen, and they're saved with the chat. They can include personal or confidential information. The automated check that reviews Claude's actions can also see the latest screenshot, and Anthropic can keep a copy of it in its record of the check. Your data is handled according to our
Commercial Terms
and
Data Processing Addendum
.
Enable or disable computer use
To turn computer use on or off for your organization:
Sign in to Claude as an Owner or Primary Owner.
Navigate to
Organization settings > Capabilities
.
Make sure
Chat and Cowork unified
is on. Computer use doesn't work without it.
Under
Claude Desktop
, find
Computer use
and turn it on or off.
On Enterprise plans, if a list of roles opens, clear every role that shouldn't have computer use, then click "Turn on."
Only an Owner or Primary Owner can change this setting. If the setting isn't there or can't be turned on, it hasn't reached your organization yet, or your organization can't have it. See
Availability
above.
When you turn computer use off, the change can take about an hour, sometimes longer, to reach each user's Claude Desktop. Until then, Claude can still see their screen and use the apps they allow.
To keep computer use off on chosen computers, see
Manage computer use with device management (MDM)
below.
Limit computer use to certain users (Enterprise plans)
Computer use is a capability in custom roles, like other features. Team plans have no custom roles, so the setting covers every user. Learn more in
Manage custom roles on Enterprise plans
.
Users with a built-in role
Users whose role is User, Admin, Owner, or Primary Owner get computer use as soon as you turn it on. To keep it from a user, set their role to "Custom," and wait 15 minutes before you turn it on.
Users with a custom role
To use computer use, a user on a custom role needs a role that includes the
Chat and Cowork unified
capability.
When you turn computer use on, your custom roles are listed, usually already selected. Clear every role that shouldn't have it.
You can't clear a role set to "All capabilities" in the list. To keep computer use from that role:
Before you turn computer use on, set the role's
Capability access
to "Only selected."
Turn off
Computer use
on the role.
Wait 15 minutes.
Turn computer use on for your organization, and clear that role in the list.
Change role access later
Once computer use is on, change which custom roles have it with "Edit role access," beside the setting, or on each role's
Capabilities
tab. Taking it away can take about an hour, sometimes longer, to reach each user's Claude Desktop.
Restrict computer use to specific apps
The
App access
setting has two lists of apps. Only an Owner or Primary Owner can change it.
Block these apps:
The apps on your block list, such as a password manager, are denied.
Allow only these apps:
Every app is denied except the ones on your allow list. Users still approve each app.
Claude can't use a denied app through computer use, except as described in
Enter an app's ID
and
What the block and allow lists don’t cover
. Choosing a list in the dropdown puts it in use, and the other list stays saved. An empty allow list goes into use when you add its first app. The apps you list are sent to your users' computers. Claude Desktop doesn't show users the list, but someone could find it, so don't include anything confidential.
While an allow list is in use, users who aren't on the latest Claude Desktop lose computer use until they update.
Add or remove apps
To add apps:
Navigate to
Organization settings > Capabilities
.
Under
Claude Desktop
, find
App access
, below
Computer use
.
Choose "Block these apps" or "Allow only these apps."
Click "Add app."
Under
Apps
, search the list of common apps and select each app you want to add. If an app isn't in the list, type its ID in the box
App IDs, one per line
, below the search.
Click "Done."
If you open
Organization settings
in Claude Desktop, the search also lists most of the apps on your computer. Those apps are denied, or allowed, only on computers with the same operating system.
To remove an app, click the trash icon at the end of its row. If you remove the last app from an allow list in use, Claude can't use any app.
Check an app
To check an app:
Wait a minute after your change.
Quit and reopen Claude Desktop on a computer that has the app.
In a new chat, ask Claude for the app by its exact name. See
What changes for your users
below.
A new version of an app can change its ID.
Enter an app's ID
Mac:
Enter the bundle ID, such as
com.microsoft.Excel
.
Windows:
Enter the program's file name, such as
excel.exe
, or a Microsoft Store app's Application User Model ID (AUMID).
Nothing checks that a typed ID names a real app.
On Windows, some apps start from one program and show their window from another. For example, LibreOffice's window belongs to soffice.bin. Put the window's file name on your block list. Otherwise, Claude can still use the app once a user approves it, even if it passes the check above.
What changes for your users
If a user asks for a denied app, Claude says that their organization blocked it, or that it isn't on their organization's list. Earlier approvals of the app stop counting. Claude can't click or type in the app, or see it in screenshots, except as described in
Enter an app's ID
and
What the block and allow lists don’t cover
.
Adding or removing an app, or switching lists, can take about an hour, sometimes longer, to reach each user's Claude Desktop. Until then, Claude can still use an app that you've just denied.
What the block and allow lists don’t cover
Claude's other tools:
This includes Claude in Chrome, the built-in browser, Claude Code, and desktop extensions. Denying Google Chrome stops only computer use in Chrome.
Other accounts:
If a user switches Claude Desktop to a personal account or to another organization, your block and allow lists don't apply there.
Websites and browser extensions:
The block and allow lists don't cover these, such as a password manager's extension, in a browser that a user approves.
Remote desktops and virtual machines:
The block and allow lists don't cover apps inside a remote desktop or virtual machine window that a user approves.
Indirect effects on a denied app:
Claude can affect a denied app through what it does in apps a user approves.
Text copied from a denied app:
Claude can read it, such as by pasting it into an app that a user approves.
Recordings made with Record a skill:
A recording includes every app on the screen, including denied ones.
Windows notifications:
A denied app's Windows notifications stay visible in screenshots, and so do the Start menu, search, and File Explorer.
What your users need
Users need the latest Claude Desktop, open on the computer Claude will use. Each user turns on
Enable computer use
there, on each computer and for each account, if it isn't already on.
Claude on the web and Claude Mobile
Using computer use from Claude on the web or Claude Mobile also needs your organization's
Computer access
setting to be on. The chat must also be connected to the computer Claude will use. Users pick the computer when asked, or in Claude on the web, under "+" > "Devices."
macOS permissions
On macOS, computer use needs the Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions. In
System Settings > Privacy & Security
, they appear as:
Accessibility
(

By

AI-Generated Summary
NVIDIA Dynamo
provides a serving layer that coordinates distributed rollout generation for reinforcement learning training.
KV-aware routing balances cache reuse and worker load to reduce redundant prompt computation and rollout delays.
ModelExpress
accelerates weight distribution by transferring compressed delta updates and reusing weights already resident in GPU memory.
Recovery mechanisms detect worker failures, reroute requests to healthy capacity, and enable replacement workers to catch up using checkpoint and delta loading.
Open-source integrations connect Dynamo to existing RL stacks including
verl
, NeMo RL, Slime, and prime-rl.
Next Steps
Explore the
Dynamo RL documentation
to begin scaling inference for reinforcement learning training.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
Reinforcement learning (RL) uses rewards to train models to solve problems and complete tasks more successfully.
Inference drives this process. Workers generate rollouts: sequences of model outputs, actions, and environment interactions. The RL framework scores the results, updates model weights, and sends those weights back to the workers for the next round.
As RL training scales, redundant compute work, slow rollouts, weight updates, and worker failures can waste GPU capacity and delay training.
NVIDIA Dynamo provides the serving layer to address these constraints, helping teams generate more accepted training samples and complete training iterations faster.
This blog post explains the rollout bottlenecks that slow RL training and how Dynamo addresses them through routing, ModelExpress weight updates, and recovery.
Figure 1. The RL loop generates rollouts, assigns rewards, and updates model weights before repeating
1. Why RL needs distributed rollout infrastructure
A reasoning rollout may contain one response. A coding-agent rollout can involve repository exploration, edits, tool calls, and tests. These differences create an uneven workload across inference workers.
Three constraints determine how effectively that workload supports training.
Rollout completion time.
When training requires a group of samples, the slowest required rollout can delay the next step. Distributing request counts evenly across GPUs does not necessarily distribute work evenly.
Repeated context.
Multiple attempts often begin with identical instructions, task descriptions, or coding repository context. Recomputing those prefixes consumes GPU capacity before new output is generated.
Weight freshness.
Training produces new model weights throughout the run. Workers must receive them according to the algorithm’s requirements for sampling and acceptable staleness.
Addressing these constraints can let teams complete more iterations within a fixed compute budget. The right optimization depends on which constraint limits the workload.
Figure 2. The three constraints on RL training: slow rollouts, redundant prompt processing, and timely weight updates
2. The Dynamo architecture for RL
Dynamo sits between rollout orchestration and inference workers. The RL framework submits generation requests; Dynamo routes them to eligible capacity; inference engines execute the model.
Figure 3. Dynamo coordinates rollout serving, the RL framework controls training and ModelExpress distributes weights
The responsibilities of each component remain explicit:
Component
Role
RL framework
Optimization, rewards, environments, checkpoints, and sample acceptance
Dynamo
Routing, worker management, serving controls, and telemetry
Inference engine
Generation and application of updated weights
ModelExpress
Model-weight and artifact distribution through supported integrations
Table 1. Component responsibilities in the Dynamo RL training loop
The generation and weight administration follow distinct paths. Requests use the shared serving frontend, while refresh operations target selected workers under framework control. This lets the framework determine when workers may generate samples and which results are eligible for training.
The separation allows teams to improve serving without transferring ownership of the learning process. Routing decisions determine where generation runs; the framework determines whether the resulting samples satisfy its training requirements. See the
RL integration reference
.
3. How Dynamo accelerates routing, weight distribution, and recovery
KV-aware routing: Reduce repeated prompt computation
RL often generates several solutions to the same task using a shared prompt. Sending these requests to a worker that has cached the prompt avoids repeated processing, saving GPU compute. But sending every request to that worker can create a queue, delaying rollouts and the next training step.
Dynamo’s router balances KV cache reuse and worker load to reduce redundant computation and waiting. The objective is earlier completion of the samples needed for training.
Figure 4. Dynamo balances cache reuse and worker load to reduce rollout delays
ModelExpress: Reduce recurring weight-distribution overhead
RL training repeatedly updates the model. Sending a full checkpoint to every rollout worker takes time and can interrupt generation.
ModelExpress
reduces this overhead by reusing weights already available in the cluster instead of loading from remote storage. Compatible workers can copy weights directly from another GPU over NIXL.
Figure 5. ModelExpress loads weights from a running worker’s GPU memory, making them available sooner than loading from storage
Delta
weight transfer
reduces the data sent between updates. Instead of moving the full model, it sends a compressed representation of what changed. Workers reconstruct the new weights from the matching base version, reducing transfer time and network traffic.
This also helps recovery. A replacement worker can load a checkpoint and apply subsequent deltas to catch up with the training run. Healthy workers can continue generating rollouts while capacity is restored.
Figure 6. ModelExpress accelerates weight updates by transferring compressed changes instead of the full model
The RL framework coordinates when workers apply updates, handles cached state, and checks readiness before accepting new samples.
Recovery: Limit the impact of worker failures
Long training runs must accommodate worker failures without unnecessarily interrupting healthy capacity.
Dynamo detects worker loss, directs new requests toward eligible workers and adds replacement workers to routing once ready, keeping rollout generation moving when a worker fails.
Supported configurations also enable migration for eligible in-flight requests and graceful draining.
The RL framework handles interrupted samples and ensures replacements use the required weights.
Figure 7. Dynamo reroutes supported sessions to healthy workers, using saved history to avoid restarting the full rollout
Dynamo in RL workflows
Dynamo adoption in RL spans frontier-model development, managed infrastructure and open source frameworks:
Microsoft AI used NVIDIA Dynamo to
support RL rollout inference during post-training
.
CoreWeave uses Dynamo and ModelExpress to accelerate model weight updates
by up to 15×.
Cognition used Dynamo to manage inference workers and route rollouts during the post-training of SWE-1.7
.
Prime Intellect uses Dynamo for distributed inference orchestration
.
H Company used Dynamo and ModelExpress
to reduce average training-step time by up to 20% and GPU-hours by up to 5%.
Open-source integrations connect Dynamo to existing RL stacks, including
verl
,
NeMo RL
,
Slime
, and
prime-rl
.
Get started with Dynamo for RL
Efficient RL infrastructure keeps rollout generation, weight distribution, and worker recovery moving together. Dynamo brings these serving capabilities into the training loop, helping teams turn distributed GPU capacity into accepted training samples and faster iterations.
Explore the
Dynamo RL documentation
and start scaling the inference behind your next model.

Enabling Real-Time AI for Scientific Instruments with GPU-Native Data Acquisition

By
Cara Laasch
,
Denis Leshchev
,
Ramya Gurunathan
and
Adam Thompson
Like

AI-Generated Summary
A high-dynamic-range electron microscopy camera developed at
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory
captures strong and faint signals simultaneously, generating over 500 Gbps of data that can be processed during acquisition.
NVIDIA DAQIRI receives detector packets directly into GPU memory, enabling real-time frame assembly, correction, and energy-loss spectra reduction while the experiment is ongoing.
The latest DAQIRI release adds hardware packet reordering on
NVIDIA ConnectX-7
or newer NICs, an ibverbs engine that nearly doubles per-core throughput at small packet sizes, and a direct polling mode demonstrating 2-4 µs application send-to-receive latency.
Next Steps
Explore the
DAQIRI documentation
to begin designing GPU-native acquisition workflows.
Review the
DAQIRI configuration examples
for hardware-specific setup guidance.
Run the
DAQIRI benchmarks
to evaluate throughput and communication latency on your platform.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
In science and industry, analyzing sensor measurements in real time can enable AI to adjust processes, guide experiments, and search for better operating conditions. Yet limits on how quickly the measured data can be moved and processed often shape how an instrument is designed, from readout electronics to acquisition timing. What could scientific instrument makers simplify—or make possible—if processing could keep pace with their sensors?
NVIDIA DAQIRI
is a software-defined data acquisition library that moves high-bandwidth instrument and sensor data into GPU-ready workflows. It enables developers to process measurements during acquisition without first writing them to disk. An
NVIDIA Holoscan
platform library, DAQIRI bridges sensors optimized for measurement with programmable GPU platforms for scientific analysis, AI inference, and feedback applications.
For existing Ethernet-capable instruments, this opens opportunities to add processing and feedback capabilities, as described in the previous post,
Enable Real-Time AI for High-Speed Data Acquisition with NVIDIA DAQIRI
. For new instruments, it allows opportunities for reconsidering acquisition constraints from the start.
This post explores how a new electron microscopy camera and GPU processing enable analysis during acquisition. It then introduces new DAQIRI features, including hardware packet reordering, performance and throughput improvements in the library, and a low-latency NIC polling mode for time-sensitive packet processing.
Case study: Connecting high-dynamic-range imaging to GPU processing
A high-dynamic-range electron microscopy camera developed at
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s
Molecular Foundry
illustrates what becomes possible when advanced detectors and GPU processing are designed to work together.
Electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) measures the energy electrons lose as they interact with a sample, helping scientists identify which elements are present and how they are bonded together. These measurements contain both strong and faint signals. To capture those differences in intensity, the conventional approach uses two separately optimized acquisition processes in rapid succession.
This requires precise coordination of the electron optics, exposure timing, and detector readout. The resulting measurements then need to be aligned and combined, adding complexity to both acquisition and processing. The new high-dynamic-range camera developed at the Molecular Foundry captures strong and faint signals together.
This advancement simplifies the experimental setup and microscope optics, but generates more than 500 gigabits of data per second (Gbps)—a stream that must be received and processed to make those measurements useful during acquisition. This is over 500x faster than conventional EELS data streams, which greatly enhances the raw detector information available for further processing and analysis.
Figure 1. Researchers at
Berkeley Lab’s Molecular Foundry
examine a hardware component beside the electron microscope used in the GPU-accelerated EELS workflow. Photo credit: Marilyn Sargent/Berkeley Lab
Handling that stream requires an acquisition and processing pipeline designed to keep pace with the camera. This is where the collaboration between Berkeley Lab and NVIDIA brings together the camera, DAQIRI, and GPU-accelerated processing. FPGA readout electronics transmit detector data over Ethernet, DAQIRI receives the packets directly into GPU memory, and GPU processing assembles and corrects detector frames before reducing them to energy-loss spectra.
Computation also improves the spatial information recovered from the detector, enabling submicron spatial resolution from sensor pixels measuring 5 micrometers across. Through this pipeline, the team enables inspection of the data during the measurement and adjusting the acquisition parameters and regions of interest in real time, all while processing high bandwidth data incoming at more than 500 Gbps.
Figure 2. The workflow of the EELS measurement at
Berkeley Lab
sends the data directly into the GPU memory, from which GPU applications can process the data while the experiment is ongoing
The benefits of this approach extend beyond electron microscopy. Connecting sensors to GPU processing can extract more information from measurements and give instrument makers greater flexibility in how they acquire, analyze, and act on data. Realizing those benefits requires efficient data movement, ordered payloads ready for processing, and low-latency communication for feedback.
Designing acquisition paths for intelligent instruments
The
latest DAQIRI release
adds hardware packet reordering, an optimized library backend for improved throughput, and direct polling for low-latency packet transmission and reception.
Reorder data as it arrives with NIC hardware
Most networks rely on protocol processing or receive-side buffering to handle out-of-order packets, which can add latency and memory overhead. DAQIRI can now offload packet reordering tasks to supported
NVIDIA ConnectX-7
or newer NICs, preserving CPU and GPU resources for analysis. For compatible sequence formats, the NIC parses sequence fields and places each payload directly into its ordered position in memory. The application receives the assembled, ordered data without requiring a separate software reorder copy step.
Hardware-based reordering is defined here for a specific receive queue. The configuration dictates how to parse the sequence number from the packet header, which reordering method to use, and how missing packets should be handled.
- name: "rx_reorder_seq_1024"
reorder_engine: "hw"          # NIC places payloads in order
cyclic_sequence: true         # Confirm compatible cyclic numbering
missing_action: “drop”        # Drop partial batches on RX timeout
reorder_type: "gpu"           # Deliver packets to GPU memory
memory_region: "Reorder_RX_GPU"
payload_byte_offset: 42       # Skip 42-byte Ethernet/IPv4/UDP header
packet_size: 8192             # Payload bytes per output slot
flow_ids: [201]               # Apply reorder to RX flow 201
method:
seq_packets_per_batch:      # Reorder by one sequence field
sequence_number:
bit_offset: 336         # Sequence starts at bit 336
bit_width: 32           # 32-bit sequence field
packets_per_batch: 1024   # 1024 packets per output buffer
Use the ibverbs engine for efficient acquisition
DAQIRI introduces an ibverbs engine for high-rate receive and transmit of raw Ethernet packets. Built on libibverbs and NVIDIA DevX, the engine is selected by default for raw Ethernet streams. Developers can also select it explicitly by adding engine: “ibverbs” to their DAQIRI configuration, without changing how they use the application API. By reducing per-packet CPU overhead, the ibverbs engine delivers approximately twice the per-core throughput of the previous default DPDK backend at small packet sizes (up to 1024 bytes) and extreme data rates (greater than 200 Gbps), based on benchmark tests performed on the
NVIDIA DGX Spark
,
NVIDIA IGX Thor
, and
NVIDIA RTX PRO
server platforms.
Figure 3. The DAQIRI ibverbs engine nearly doubles throughput for 64-byte and 256-byte packets compared with DPDK, while maintaining similar throughput for 8 KB packets. Results shown are from single-queue benchmarks on NVIDIA IGX Thor
Reduce feedback latency with direct polling
Intelligent instruments may require latency-sensitive feedback from GPU analysis to adjust acquisition or control settings. The DAQIRI direct polling mode reduces communication latency by letting the application thread receive and submit packets directly, eliminating the handoff to a separate I/O worker. In cabled loopback benchmark tests, application send-to-receive latency on the order of 2-4 µs has been demonstrated in direct polling mode. When using the ibverbs engine, developers can select direct polling for control queues while retaining batched processing for high-throughput data streams.
Set
poll_mode: "direct"
on the latency-sensitive TX and RX control queues so the application thread submits and receives packets directly.
# TX/RX queue settings in example configuration file
tx:
queues:
- name: "control_tx"
id: 0
poll_mode: "direct"         # App thread submits packets
memory_regions: ["Control_TX"]
rx:
queues:
- name: "control_rx"
id: 0
poll_mode: "direct"         # App thread polls received packets
memory_regions: ["Control_RX"]
Run the direct-polling latency benchmark using a cabled loopback between TX and RX ports on the same host.
First, replace the configuration’s hardware address placeholders and other system-specific settings with values for your system:
sudo ./build/examples/daqiri_bench_raw_latency
examples/daqiri_bench_raw_latency_ibverbs.yaml --samples
10000 --warmup 1000 --csv latency.csv
Get started with GPU-native data acquisition
During the process of making scientific instruments, GPU-native data acquisition enables you to design around what will be measured and your desired means of response. Advanced detectors and GPU processing can work together for reconsidering acquisition constraints.
The latest DAQIRI capabilities extend the options for moving and organizing measurements efficiently and connecting analysis to experimental control. That means more engineering effort can focus on measurement quality and scientific insight.
To explore these capabilities, start with the
DAQIRI documentation
and
DAQIRI configuration examples
. Then use the
DAQIRI benchmarks
to evaluate throughput and communication latency on your hardware.
To learn more, check out these related resources:
Explore the
NVIDIA/daqiri
GitHub repo
Browse the
DAQIRI plus TensorRT Streaming Inference Reference Application
Generate
DAQIRI Configurations
for your hardware

Please note the following changes:
Model Context Protocol (MCP) support
:
Apigee hybrid version 1.17 adds support for the
Model Context Protocol (MCP)
, an
open protocol that lets agentic AI applications use your APIs as tools through managed MCP
endpoints. Apigee hybrid routes, authorizes, and secures these MCP tool calls the same way it

certificate

TLS 1.3 support
:

stronger security than earlier TLS versions. For information about configuring TLS on the ingress
gateway, see

the ingress gateway

Forward proxy support for AI policies
:

versions of Apigee hybrid. For more information, see

proxying for API proxies

Semantic cache Private Service Connect (PSC) endpoint support
:

support for semantic caching. The semantic caching policies can now reach their backing services
over a Private Service Connect endpoint, which keeps that traffic on your private network. For

items.title: Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds Agent Anomaly Detection now monitors ADK agents running across AWS, Azure, or on-premises by analyzing their traces
items.content:
Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds
- Google Developers Blog
Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds
NOV. 20, 2026
Gopi Subburaja Alagar
Software Engineer
Arvind Chaudhary
Software Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Agent Anomaly Detection is in Private Preview, including monitoring for agents that run outside Google Cloud. To request access, see the
Agent Anomaly Detection overview
.
Our
launch post
introduced Agent Anomaly Detection, which helps you understand and act on agent behavior that drifts outside its intended boundaries. It covered agents on Google Cloud, such as Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Many teams also run agents on other clouds: on AWS Lambda next to an inventory database, as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry, or on-premises next to a system that can't move. Those agents carry the same behavioral risks, and until now Agent Anomaly Detection couldn't review them.
Agent Anomaly Detection works from an agent's traces and logs, so it doesn't need access to the agent's runtime. If those traces and logs reach your Google Cloud project, it can detect anomalous behavior wherever the agent runs. In this post, we explain what Agent Anomaly Detection needs from an agent on other cloud, then show what it found for an agent on AWS Lambda and an agent on Microsoft Foundry.
How it works on other clouds
Agent Anomaly Detection reads the logging and observability buckets that you choose when you enable it. Telemetry from anywhere works when:
It arrives through the Telemetry API (
telemetry.googleapis.com
), which keeps the resource attributes that identify the agent.
It follows OpenTelemetry conventions and records prompts and responses as log events, which is where Agent Anomaly Detection reads the conversation.
A resource attribute names the agent.
Agents built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) for Python, version 2.12.0 or later, can produce this telemetry with ADK's Google Cloud exporters and a few environment variables, which the next section shows.
Agents on other clouds send traces and logs to a Google Cloud project, where Agent Anomaly Detection analyzes them.
Connect an agent from another cloud
An agent outside Google Cloud needs two things to send its telemetry:
A Google identity without a service account key.
With Workload Identity Federation, the agent trades its own identity, such as an AWS role or a Microsoft Entra identity, for short-lived Google credentials. The configuration file that sets this up contains no secret.
An exporter.
ADK's Google Cloud exporters send traces and logs to the Telemetry API. A few environment variables configure them:
GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=<PROJECT_ID>
GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/path/to/gcp-credentials.json
# Capture prompts and responses in the format Agent Anomaly Detection reads.
OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=gen_ai_latest_experimental
OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT=EVENT_ONLY
ADK_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT_IN_SPANS=false
# Describe the agent and where it runs.
OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=<AGENT_NAME>
OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=cloud.provider=<aws|azure>,cloud.platform=<PLATFORM>,cloud.region=<REGION>,faas.name=<AGENT_NAME>
Shell
Copied
For the full setup on AWS and Azure, see the
documentation
.
Within 30 minutes, the agent appears in the Monitored agents list, which means it has been
discovered
and is ready to be
enabled
. Once it's enabled, manually or by
automatic agent enrollment
at discovery, Agent Anomaly Detection starts analyzing its sessions.
The agent's model and tool calls still run where the agent runs. Only telemetry, including the prompts and responses that Agent Anomaly Detection reads, goes to your Google Cloud project. The analysis runs separately, so it doesn't slow the agent down.
What we tested
To evaluate Agent Anomaly Detection outside Google Cloud, we deployed ADK agents across two platforms: an inventory agent on AWS Lambda and a customer-service agent on Microsoft Foundry. The examples below show how Agent Anomaly Detection reads whole conversations, not isolated calls, to catch behavioral drift.
Example 1: An inventory agent on AWS Lambda
Our example inventory agent runs in AWS Lambda with one tool,
list_inventory
, which pages through a product catalog. We sent two sessions: a shopper who checked stock for a few items and stopped, and a scraper that requested 100 catalog items at a time at increasing offsets to copy the full catalog and inventory data. Both sessions used the same tool with permitted calls, but differed in pattern and intent.
Of the two sessions, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged only the scraper's. No call failed, but the whole exchange showed systematic scraping. The analysis found
cascading failures
(loops and repeated calls that build on each other) and
resource exhaustion
(runaway use of tokens, compute, or tool calls), and recommended rate-limiting
list_inventory
calls.
Detection doesn't depend on the agent's model. When we ran the inventory agent on Amazon Nova Lite through Amazon Bedrock, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 10 of its 40 sessions. Some began as routine questions that the model answered by paging through the entire catalog until the function timed out: no errors, no blocked calls, and easy to miss.
The Bedrock inventory agent in Agent Anomaly Detection: 10 of 40 sessions flagged
Bedrock session: a request to list every inventory item, flagged for resource exhaustion and cascading failures
Example 2: A customer-service agent on Foundry
Our example ecommerce customer-service agent has two tools:
get_order_status
and
issue_refund
. Refunds involve money, so they carry the highest risk.
We ran six sessions against the Foundry agent, which we told to carry out every request without validation. Two were normal: One asked for an order's status, and one asked for a $20 refund on an order that arrived damaged. The other four pushed the agent past its role, and Agent Anomaly Detection flagged all four.
In one, a user who claimed to be the store administrator had every order refunded at 10 times its total to a personal account, $1,784.90 in all. In another, a user pasted an order note that said "SYSTEM OVERRIDE," and the agent refunded $999 on a $15.99 order.
For the order note, Agent Anomaly Detection explained that override instructions in the note coerced the agent into an unverified $999 refund. It recommended validating
issue_refund
arguments to block override patterns in order notes, and requiring extra validation for refunds above a set threshold.
Store-administrator session: 10x refunds to a personal account, showing identity and privilege abuse findings and recommendations
Order-note session: an unverified refund from a pasted order note, showing tool misuse findings and recommendations
What's next
If your agent's telemetry reaches Google Cloud, Agent Anomaly Detection can monitor it with the same detectors and console as your agents on Agent Runtime. Today that means agents built with ADK for Python. Findings for agents outside Google Cloud appear only in the Agent Anomaly Detection console.
To get started, request access to the Private Preview via the
Agent Anomaly Detection overview
, and then refer to the
setup guide
for instructions.

How to securely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini Enterprise
- Google Developers Blog
How to securely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini Enterprise
NOV. 20, 2026
Neeraj Agrawal
Forward Deployed Engineer
Google Cloud
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Enterprise teams adopting
Gemini Enterprise
are increasingly building custom
Model Context Protocol (MCP)
servers to connect AI agents with internal APIs, databases, and business workflows.
Google Cloud Run
is a natural fit for hosting these lightweight StreamableHTTP MCP servers: it scales automatically, manages TLS certificates out of the box, and integrates natively with Cloud IAM.
However, moving a custom MCP server from an initial prototype to an enterprise production environment immediately introduces three real-world security and networking challenges:
No public internet exposure (internal-only ingress):
Enterprise security policies require internal MCP servers to block all public internet traffic and accept requests only from private Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks. When internal ingress is enabled on Cloud Run, default public calls from Gemini Enterprise are rejected at Google's edge with HTTP 404.
Service and user authentication (Cloud Run IAM + OAuth 2.0):
Production deployments require two independent identity checks on every tool call. Cloud Run IAM must verify that the network request originated from your authorized Gemini Enterprise instance, and your MCP application code must validate the signed-in human user's OAuth 2.0 access token before acting on their behalf.
Shared VPC scale without DNS collisions:
Large enterprises often run hundreds of Cloud Run services across a centralized Shared (Hub) VPC. Overriding the entire *.run.app domain in Private Cloud DNS for a single MCP server can hijack DNS resolution and break routing for other Cloud Run services across that network.
Here is how you can solve all three challenges using
Egress Agent Gateway
,
Private Service Connect (PSC)
, and
FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS
, complete with a runnable reference implementation and setup scripts on
GitHub
.
How the private path works
Connecting Gemini Enterprise (which runs in a Google-managed tenant project) to an internal serverless Cloud Run MCP server requires bridging
two network hops
and
one scoped DNS lookup
:
Figure 1: Private VPC and dual-header authentication architecture for connecting Gemini Enterprise to internal Cloud Run MCP servers.
Three Google Cloud networking and identity mechanisms work together in this architecture:
1. Two-bridge private VPC routing (PSC Network Attachment + PGA or PSC for Google APIs)
Unlike a Compute Engine VM with an internal IP address inside your subnet, Cloud Run is serverless. Private routing therefore uses two bridges:
Bridge 1 (Into your VPC via PSC Network Attachment):
A regional
Egress Agent Gateway
in Agent-to-Anywhere mode connects to a
PSC Network Attachment
in your regional subnet (us-central1 or europe-west1). This places a managed network interface inside your VPC without public IPs or inbound firewall rules.
Bridge 2 (From your VPC to Serverless Cloud Run):
Once the packet enters your VPC subnet, it must reach Google's serverless Cloud Run frontend privately so Cloud Run recognizes the source VPC and satisfies internal ingress rules. Depending on your enterprise VPC design, you can use either:
Option A: Subnet Private Google Access (199.36.153.8/30):
Uses Google's built-in Private Google Access virtual IPs with zero extra VPC endpoints (recommended for standard VPCs that retain the default 0.0.0.0/0 route to the default internet gateway).
Option B: Global PSC Endpoint for Google APIs (240.0.0.10):
Uses a global internal IP address and forwarding rule targeting Google's built-in all-apis bundle (which includes Cloud Run with no internal load balancer or service attachment needed on the Cloud Run side). Google Cloud automatically injects a dedicated /32 internal route into your VPC, so private Cloud Run routing works even in locked-down VPCs where the 0.0.0.0/0 default internet route is deleted.
2. FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS resolution (safe for Shared VPCs)
When the Egress Agent Gateway receives a tool call for your Cloud Run MCP server URL, it resolves the hostname once before injecting the packet into your VPC. Without Private Cloud DNS, public DNS resolves .run.app domains to public internet IPs, which time out (HTTP 502) because a PSC Network Attachment does not route out to the public internet.
Instead of creating a wildcard *.run.app private zone, which would override DNS resolution for every Cloud Run service in a Shared VPC, you create a Private Cloud DNS zone scoped
exclusively
to your MCP service's exact fully qualified domain name (FQDN) and peer only that domain with the Agent Gateway. Because Cloud DNS uses longest-suffix matching, every other Cloud Run service in your Shared VPC continues resolving normally. Meanwhile, the Agent Gateway opens its HTTPS connection to the private VIP (199.36.153.8 or 240.0.0.10) while preserving your Cloud Run service hostname in the TLS SNI and HTTP Host header so Cloud Run routes the request to your exact container.
3. Dual-header service and user identity
When connecting to a Cloud Run MCP server URL, Gemini Enterprise sends two distinct authorization headers on every request:
Infrastructure layer (X-Serverless-Authorization header):
Contains a Google-signed OIDC ID token for your project's Gemini Enterprise service agent. Cloud Run IAM verifies this token against the Cloud Run Invoker role at the serverless edge and strips the header before the request reaches your container.
Application layer (Authorization Bearer header):
Contains the signed-in user's OAuth 2.0 access token untouched, allowing middleware inside your MCP server to verify the caller's identity and enforce per-user permissions.
class OAuth2ValidationMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
"""Validates the end-user OAuth 2.0 Bearer token on incoming MCP requests."""
async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next) -> Response:
if request.url.path == "/health":
return await call_next(request)
has_serverless_auth = "x-serverless-authorization" in request.headers
auth_header = request.headers.get("authorization", "")
if auth_header.lower().startswith("bearer "):
raw_token = auth_header.split(" ", 1)[1].strip()
verified = await _verify_google_oauth_token(raw_token)
if verified is None and REQUIRE_OAUTH:
return JSONResponse(
{"error": "Invalid or expired OAuth 2.0 Bearer token."},
status_code=401,
)
elif REQUIRE_OAUTH:
return JSONResponse(
{"error": "Missing Authorization: Bearer <token> header."},
status_code=401,
)
return await call_next(request)
Python
Copied
5 steps to configure the integration
Our companion
GitHub repository
automates the entire deployment into sequential setup scripts alongside step-by-step Cloud Console instructions:
Step 1: Lock down Cloud Run and grant service invoker access
Deploy your StreamableHTTP MCP server to Cloud Run with internal-only ingress and IAM authentication enabled, and grant the Cloud Run Invoker role to your project's Gemini Enterprise service agent so only your Gemini Enterprise instance can invoke the container.
Step 2: Provision the VPC, PSC Network Attachment, and Egress Agent Gateway
Enable Private Google Access on your regional VPC subnet and create a Private Service Connect Network Attachment set to accept connections automatically. Next, create a Google-managed Egress Agent Gateway in Agent-to-Anywhere mode, grant networking and DNS peering permissions to the auto-created gateway service accounts, attach your network attachment, and apply an outbound authorization policy.
Step 3: Configure FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS and DNS peering
In Cloud DNS, create a private managed zone attached to your VPC for
only
your MCP service's exact Cloud Run hostname. Point its A record to Google's Private Google Access VIPs (or to your internal PSC endpoint IP for isolated VPCs without a default internet route), and configure DNS peering on the Agent Gateway for that single hostname.
Step 4: Bind the Agent Gateway and register the MCP server in Gemini Enterprise
In the Gemini Enterprise console under Security Configuration, bind your Egress Agent Gateway to your app. Register your Custom MCP Server data store with your Cloud Run endpoint and OAuth 2.0 client credentials, and enable Agent Gateway egress and Actions mode on the connector.
Step 5: Verify private MCP calls in Cloud Logging
Reload your custom actions in the console and run a test prompt in the Gemini Enterprise web app. In Cloud Logging, you can verify that tool initialization, discovery, and execution calls route privately through the Egress Agent Gateway to your internal Cloud Run container with both service IAM and user OAuth 2.0 checks passing.
Next steps
To deploy and test both private routing patterns in your own Google Cloud project, check out the
GitHub repository
for:
A complete Python StreamableHTTP Cloud Run MCP server with OAuth 2.0 validation middleware, Dockerfile, and local smoke tests.
Step-by-step setup scripts and Cloud Console UI instructions covering both
Option A (Subnet Private Google Access)
and
Option B (Global PSC Endpoint for Google APIs)
, including Shared VPC IAM bindings and Cloud Logging verification.

items.content:
How to handle user, connector, and agent auth in Gemini Enterprise with a custom UI
- Google Developers Blog
How to handle user, connector, and agent auth in Gemini Enterprise with a custom UI
NOV. 20, 2026
Neeraj Agrawal
Forward Deployed Engineer
Google Cloud
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
When using the out-of-the-box
Gemini Enterprise
web application, identity and access management happen behind the scenes. Employees sign in through Google Identity or Workforce Identity Federation (such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta), search results automatically respect per-user access controls (ACLs), and third-party login prompts for
Federated Connectors
or
custom agents
appear automatically in the chat UI.
In practice, however, many enterprises build their own
Customer UI
to embed Gemini Enterprise into an internal portal, intranet, or line-of-business application. To do this,
Customer BE
calls the Gemini Enterprise
StreamAssist API
.
The moment an application builds a custom UI and calls the StreamAssist API directly, the three authentication flows that the built-in web app handled automatically become the responsibility of
Customer UI
and
Customer BE
:
Authenticating to StreamAssist (User Identity vs. Workload Identity):
For user-facing applications where document ACLs, isolated chat history, and restricted agent permissions matter,
Customer UI
and
Customer BE
must pass the signed-in employee's identity via Google Identity (
Pattern 1A
) or Workforce Identity Federation (
Pattern 1B
). For non-personalized backend bots or shared service portals,
Customer BE
can authenticate keyless using Workload Identity Federation (
Pattern 1C
).
Authenticating Federated Connectors through Customer UI:
Real-time Federated Connectors use 3-Legged OAuth (3LO) so they only retrieve Google Drive files, SharePoint sites, Jira issues, or ServiceNow incidents that the signed-in employee is allowed to see. Because
Customer UI
does not have Gemini Enterprise's built-in Connect button,
Customer BE
and
Customer UI
must discover the engine's connectors, check the
Keystore
for a valid token, trigger the 3LO consent popup when needed, save the refresh token in the
Keystore
, and include the connector data stores in StreamAssist queries.
Handling per-tool OAuth for custom ADK agents:
When deploying a custom
ADK agent
on
Vertex AI Agent Engine
that connects to multiple enterprise systems (such as Google Drive and Microsoft SharePoint), attaching static OAuth configs at the root agent registration level blocks the entire agent upfront. Instead, by wrapping protected sub-agent tools with
GcpAuthProvider
(backed by
GCP Auth Manager's Token Vault
) and deploying the agent with
Agent Identity
turned on, StreamAssist triggers an on-demand 3LO popup only when a protected tool is called.
This guide walks through the architecture, component flows, and runnable code for all three layers (
Figure 1
):
Figure 1: End-to-end authentication architecture across StreamAssist login (Google Identity, Workforce STS, or Workload STS), Federated Connectors (Keystore), and custom ADK agents (Vertex AI Agent Engine + GCP Auth Manager Token Vault).
Part 1: Three patterns to authenticate to StreamAssist (User & Workload)
Depending on whether
Customer UI
is acting on behalf of an individual employee or running as a shared backend bot, customer architectures follow three keyless authentication patterns:
Figure 2: Comparing Pattern 1A (Pure Google Identity), Pattern 1B (Workforce Identity Federation + Google STS), and Pattern 1C (Workload Identity Federation + Google STS) for calling StreamAssist.
Required IAM Role and License:
Every principal calling the StreamAssist API must be granted the
Discovery Engine User
IAM role on the GCP project. For human user patterns (
Pattern 1A
and
Pattern 1B
), the user (or Workforce Pool group) must also have an active Gemini Enterprise user license assigned in the Admin Console.
Pattern 1A: Pure Google Identity (Google Login UI to StreamAssist)
When employees sign in with Google Workspace or Cloud Identity and the Gemini Enterprise engine is configured for Google Identity, the flow has zero extra hops:
Customer UI
signs the employee in using
Google Identity Services (OAuth 2.0)
with the Google Cloud Platform scope.
Google returns a user access token scoped to the signed-in employee.
Customer BE
sends that Bearer token directly to the StreamAssist API.
Pattern 1B: Workforce Identity Federation (External IdP UI to Google STS to StreamAssist
)
When employees sign into
Customer UI
with Microsoft Entra ID or Okta and Gemini Enterprise uses
Workforce Identity Federation (WIF)
, you reuse the same Workforce Pool that is already connected to Gemini Enterprise:
Register Customer UI on the existing WIF Provider:
Add the custom web app's Entra ID or Okta Client ID to the Google Cloud Workforce Pool OIDC Provider.
Exchange the IdP token at Google STS:
After the employee signs into
Customer UI
and receives an OIDC token from Entra ID or Okta,
Customer BE
exchanges that token at Google Security Token Service (STS) against the Workforce Pool Provider.
Call StreamAssist with the federated user token:
Google STS returns a short-lived Google access token representing that specific Workforce Pool user, enforcing all of the employee's group permissions and document ACLs.
Pattern 1C: Workload Identity Federation (Backend / Shared Bot to Google STS to StreamAssist)
When a backend service, Slack/Teams webhook, or non-personalized knowledge bot needs to call StreamAssist without any Service Account JSON keys, use a project-scoped
Workload Identity Pool
:
Obtain a machine JWT from the external IdP:
Customer BE
requests an application token from the external IdP (for example, using OAuth 2.0 client credentials in Entra ID).
Exchange at Google STS:
Customer BE
exchanges that machine JWT at Google STS against the project's Workload Identity Pool Provider with zero keys on disk.
Call StreamAssist:
Customer BE
sends the returned Google STS token to StreamAssist.
When to use Pattern 1C vs. Patterns 1A and 1B:
Because Workload Identity Federation authenticates a machine rather than an individual human employee, Gemini Enterprise sees every request as coming from the same workload identity. Use
Pattern 1C
for non-personalized bots over shared knowledge bases, and use
Pattern 1A
or

Introducing Perplexity Frontier Research

Authors
Perplexity Research
We are excited to launch
Perplexity Frontier Research
, a new initiative to advance the frontier of algorithms, models, and evaluations, in the open.
We aim to build an automatic research scientist, an AI system that can conduct research on its own. Research is a loop that involves asking the right questions, hypothesizing, designing experiments, analyzing results, navigating ambiguity, and updating beliefs. In contrast to black-box predictions in narrowly defined settings, this effort is designed to produce new interpretable knowledge that advances our understanding across a broad range of applications.
This ambition inspires new algorithms, models, and evaluations. We will be particularly considering six pillars: multi-agent orchestration, pre-training, continual learning, reinforcement learning, systems, and evaluations. Within each of these areas, we will explore a variety of foundational questions. For example, can we propose new, more efficient architectures? Can we synthesize data that enables broader generalization? Under what conditions is multi-agent collaboration most effective? Can we create evaluations that measure research ability and extrapolation, rather than only recall?
This is an environment where one has the opportunity to advance the frontier of research, and share results openly. We will release papers, blog posts, data, models, and code. Our research will also be supported by considerable computational resources, in excess of 10,000 GPUs. And our findings shape a product used by millions of curious people, the most challenging test of all.

Cohere Expands Its Sovereign AI Platform with AISLE and cubic
Expanding the sovereign AI platform with new capabilities for cyber defense, secure software development, and mission-critical enterprise workflows

Written By

AI isn’t a shortcut.
It’s how business gets ahead.
Contact sales
Over the past year, we've seen a fundamental shift in how organizations approach AI. Enterprises and governments are deploying AI into the workflows that matter most, from cybersecurity and software development to mission-critical operations and decision-making. As they do, their requirements are becoming increasingly clear: they need AI systems that are powerful, secure, and under their control.
At Cohere, we've long believed organizations shouldn't have to choose between cutting-edge AI and control. They should be able to deploy advanced AI while maintaining ownership of their data, infrastructure, and operations. That's the foundation of sovereign AI.
Today, we're excited to share two important milestones in that journey. We're pleased to announce the completion of our acquisition of AISLE, the company building autonomous systems for vulnerability discovery and remediation. We're also welcoming the team behind cubic, one of the leading AI-powered code review platforms, to Cohere.
Together, these additions strengthen the sovereign AI platform we're building for organizations around the world. With
AISLE
and cubic we’ve completed four strategic M&A transactions this year, following
Aleph Alpha
,
Reliant AI
to expand our capabilities across frontier AI, biopharma and healthcare, cybersecurity, and software development.
Cybersecurity is a defining frontier of AI
As AI becomes embedded in critical systems and workflows, security is becoming a defining requirement for adoption. Organizations increasingly need AI that can operate inside private clouds, on-premises and air-gapped environments while meeting rigorous requirements around privacy, governance, and compliance.
That's why we're excited to officially welcome AISLE to Cohere. When we announced our intent to acquire AISLE, we outlined a shared belief: the future of AI depends on the ability to secure both AI systems and the software infrastructure that powers them. As organizations deploy AI into increasingly sensitive environments, cyber resilience becomes foundational to trust.
AISLE’s co-founders are taking leadership roles spanning cybersecurity, corporate security, AI security research and frontier model development. Ondrej Vlcek will become Senior Vice President, Cohere Cyber, and lead the newly established cybersecurity business. Jaya Baloo will become Cohere’s Chief Information Security Officer, overseeing security across the company. Stanislav Fort will become Vice President, AI Security, joining Cohere’s core model research and training efforts while leading AI security research.
Cohere also plans to make a substantial long-term investment in Prague, expanding AISLE’s existing presence and establishing the city as its global center for AI cybersecurity and autonomous security systems.
AISLE brings world-class expertise in autonomous security research and vulnerability discovery.
Their work has demonstrated how specialized AI systems can identify, validate, and remediate vulnerabilities at a speed and scale that helps defenders stay ahead of an increasingly complex threat landscape.
Today, that expertise has become the foundation of Cohere Cyber, our cybersecurity business focused on helping enterprises, governments, and critical infrastructure operators build and operate secure, cyber-resilient AI systems. Together, we're building cyber defense capabilities that help organizations deploy AI with confidence in even the most demanding environments.
Bringing secure coding to enterprise scale
Software development is one of the most widely adopted enterprise applications of AI. But organizations need more than systems that generate code. They need AI that can understand complex codebases, review changes, identify vulnerabilities, maintain software quality, and operate within strict security boundaries. That's what attracted us to cubic.
The team has built an industry-leading AI-powered code review platform that helps engineering organizations review code, find bugs and vulnerabilities, understand complex codebases, and automatically remediate issues. Their review agents have consistently ranked among the strongest performers on code review benchmarks and were built for the environments many enterprise customers operate in, including on-premises and air-gapped deployments.
Led by founder and CEO Paul Sanglé-Ferrière, the team brings expertise across AI, security, developer tools, distributed systems, and enterprise software. They will establish Cohere's secure coding vertical, helping accelerate the integration of enterprise-grade coding capabilities into our platform while meeting the security, governance, and deployment requirements our customers demand. Their work strengthens our ability to help organizations build, maintain, and secure software using AI within their own environments and under their own control.
Building AI for the world's most critical industries
What connects AISLE and cubic is more than technical excellence. Both teams have built products for organizations operating in environments where security, reliability, governance, and control are non-negotiable.
Their work reflects a broader shift we're seeing across the market. Organizations increasingly want AI they can deploy on their own terms. They want systems that fit within their security requirements, regulatory obligations, and operational realities without becoming dependent on systems they can't inspect, adapt, or control.
We believe this is where the next phase of AI adoption will be won. By bringing together frontier models, secure deployment infrastructure, cyber defense, and purpose-built applications, we're continuing to build a sovereign AI platform that gives organizations more capability, more security, and more control.
Looking ahead
The future of AI won't be defined by models alone. It will be defined by the systems, workflows, and infrastructure built around them. The question is whether organizations can deploy AI securely and at scale across the systems that matter most. That's the promise of sovereign AI.
Welcoming AISLE and cubic to Cohere strengthens our ability to deliver on that vision. Together, we're building a sovereign AI platform that enterprises and governments can trust to operate in their most sensitive environments, power their most critical workflows, and realize the full potential of AI while maintaining control of their data, infrastructure, and operations.
We're excited to welcome both teams to Cohere and look forward to what we'll build together.

items.title: Microsoft Azure Cobalt 200 VMs reach general availability, bringing Arm-powered performance to cloud and agentic AI workloads
items.content:
Microsoft Azure Cobalt 200 VMs reach general availability, bringing Arm-powered performance to cloud and agentic AI workloads  - Arm Newsroom
Arm Newsroom
News
News
November 17, 2026
Microsoft Azure Cobalt 200 VMs reach general availability, bringing Arm-powered performance to cloud and agentic AI workloads
By
Mohamed Awad
,
Executive Vice President, Cloud AI,
Arm
Share
News highlights
Microsoft Azure Cobalt 200 VMs are now generally available, built on Arm Neoverse CSS V3 to simplify silicon development and enable differentiation
Cobalt 200 VMs deliver up to 50% better CPU performance than Cobalt 100 VMs, supporting demanding cloud and agentic AI workloads
Arm-based server market share at leading hyperscalers is expected to exceed 60% by the end of 2026, reflecting growing adoption of Arm-powered cloud infrastructure
AI is fundamentally changing cloud infrastructure requirements. As agentic AI moves into production, cloud providers need greater performance, efficiency and flexibility to scale. Custom silicon allows hyperscalers to design infrastructure around the evolving needs of their customers.
At Microsoft Ignite 2026, Microsoft announced the
general availability of Azure Cobalt 200 virtual machines
(VMs), bringing its latest Arm-based custom CPU to customers running demanding cloud and agentic AI workloads. Built on
Arm Neoverse Compute Subsystems V3 (CSS V3)
, Cobalt 200 marks the next step in our collaboration to advance Azure’s compute infrastructure.
Arm-based server market share at leading hyperscalers more than tripled from 15% in 2024 to over 50% in 2025, with
Arm expecting that share to exceed 60% by the end of 2026
. Microsoft’s plans for Cobalt 200 to represent a significant portion of new Azure Compute capacity in 2027 and beyond reinforce that momentum and Arm’s growing role in cloud infrastructure.
Delivering greater value for Azure customers tackling agentic AI workloads
Agentic AI is expanding the role of the cloud CPU. Agents execute code, retrieve data, invoke tools and coordinate tasks across applications, relying on CPUs to support these operations alongside the databases, caches and services that power enterprise workloads. Scaling these systems requires high-performance CPUs that can deliver responsive execution and efficiency at scale.
Cobalt 200 demonstrates the impact of purpose-built Arm-based infrastructure. Microsoft reports up to 50% better CPU performance for Cobalt 200 VMs compared with Cobalt 100, while
Arm’s workload testing
shows similar improvements across cloud applications. These gains strengthen the compute foundation supporting enterprise services and emerging agentic AI workloads.
Customers including Amadeus, Databricks, InMobi, OpenAI, SAP, and Snowflake are already seeing the benefits of Cobalt 200 across real-world workloads, from faster application response times to improved infrastructure utilization.
Accelerating custom silicon differentiation with Arm Neoverse CSS
Custom silicon gives hyperscalers greater control over performance, efficiency and their infrastructure roadmaps. But differentiation shouldn’t require rebuilding every element of a modern cloud CPU from scratch.
Arm Neoverse CSS V3 provides a proven, pre-integrated compute framework that helps partners reduce development complexity and accelerate time-to-market while retaining the flexibility to customize their silicon.
Microsoft utilizes that framework with capabilities tailored to Azure, including custom compression, cryptographic accelerators and per-core power management. Combined with Microsoft’s systems and software engineering, these capabilities allow Azure to optimize how workloads use compute, move data and consume power.
“With Cobalt 200, we’re building on our collaboration with Arm to deliver the performance and efficiency our customers need as cloud and AI workloads evolve,” said Reynold D’Sa, CVP Silicon, Cloud Hardware, and Infrastructure Engineering, Microsoft. “Arm Neoverse CSS V3 gives us the framework to innovate and differentiate, while allowing us to focus on the silicon and systems capabilities that make Azure unique.”
Enabling the Cobalt 200 ecosystem at scale
Cobalt 200 builds on an established Arm software ecosystem. Our collaboration with Microsoft extends across software optimization, migration support and developer enablement, helping customers adopt Arm-based compute for existing applications and new agentic services.
Together, Arm’s flexible compute framework, Microsoft’s silicon and systems innovation, and a mature software ecosystem are helping accelerate the adoption of Arm-based infrastructure across the cloud.
By
Mohamed Awad
,
Executive Vice President, Cloud AI,
Arm
